teach.title: Long by nature

notice.ask: *spectant* in one line and *noster* in the other both begin with a short vowel. What do their first syllables have in common?
options: Both count long, because two consonants follow the vowel
Both count short, because the vowel is short
Both count long, because the vowel has a macron
notice.answer: Both count long, because two consonants follow the vowel

teach.say: Before a line can be cut into feet you need **prosody (which syllables count long or short, and when a final vowel is swallowed by the next word)**. A syllable is long if its vowel is long (the macron shows it) or holds a diphthong, two vowels said as one: *ae, au, oe, eu*. Everything else starts out short.

check.ask: Tap the word whose two syllables are both long because both hold a diphthong.

teach.title: Long by position
teach.say: The second rule surprises people: a syllable with a *short* vowel counts long when two consonants follow it. In *spectant* the *e* is short, yet *spec-* is a long syllable, because *c* and *t* come after it. The second consonant may even belong to the next word: *sub lūce* makes *sub* long, because *b* and *l* meet across the gap.

check.ask: Tap the word that describes pater: its o is a short vowel, yet its first syllable counts long.

teach.title: Elision: a swallowed vowel
teach.say: When a word ends in a vowel, or in a vowel + *m*, and the next word begins with a vowel or with *h-*, that ending is swallowed and not counted. This is elision, and it is why a line that looks too long scans perfectly. English does it too: say 'the end' quickly and you get 'th'end'.

check.ask: Tap the word that loses its last letter to the word after it.

teach.title: Putting it together
teach.say: Copy the line out, cross out every elision, then mark long over each long vowel, each diphthong and each syllable long by position, and short over the rest. Divide from the *end*, where the pattern is fixed. If the feet will not come out, your marking is wrong: look for a missed elision or a syllable long by position.

check.ask: Tap the word that fills the fifth foot exactly, one whole word to one whole dactyl.

core.text: To read verse aloud you need **prosody (which syllables count long or short, and when a final vowel is swallowed by the next word)**. (1) A syllable is long if its vowel is long (*ā*) or a diphthong (*ae, au, oe, eu*). (2) It is long 'by position' if two consonants follow, even across words; *x* counts as two, *h* as none. (3) Elision: a final vowel, or vowel + *m*, is dropped before a vowel or *h*: *Ōd(ī) et amō*; *Lesbi(a) atqu(e) amēmus*. Latin name: *prosōdia: quantitās syllabārum, ēlīsiō*.
Say *the end* fast: *th'end* — that is elision. 'Long' is about time, not loudness.
Mark each syllable long or short, bracket elided vowels, then cut into feet. Final -ō is sometimes short (amŏ, nēmŏ).

invented.la: Bella puella redit, sed nēmō vīdit amantem.
invented.en: A pretty girl comes back, but no one has seen her lover. (a made-up hexameter: – ⏑ ⏑ | – ⏑ ⏑ | – – | – – | – ⏑ ⏑ | – –)

core.text: Ovid (Week 13): *Saepe me|ae 'Tan|dem' dī|xī 'dis|cēde' pu|ellae* — dactyl, three spondees, dactyl, spondee (*Sae-*, *-ae* diphthongs; *dis-* long before *c*; *pu-* short); *in gremi|ō sē|dit || prōtinus | illa me|ō* — *in* long before *n* + *gr*.
Metre says what pattern to expect; prosody says what each syllable is. When they disagree, recheck the prosody: usually a missed elision or a long-by-position syllable.

more.text: Martial's couplet (Week 14) scanned: *Nōn amo | tē, Sabi|dī, nec | possum | dīcere | quārē* and *Hoc tan|tum pos|sum || dīcere | nōn amo | tē*: *amō* twice with its *-ō* counted short, *nec* long before *p*, *Hoc* long before *t*, *tum* long before *p*. Elision at work in Catullus: *Vīvāmus, mea Lesbia, atque amēmus* reads *Lesbi(a) atqu(e) amēmus*. With *est* and *es* it is the *e* of the little verb that drops after a vowel or *-s* (*sōla est* → *sōla'st*, *bella es* → *bella's*). Not every meeting of vowels elides: *passer mortuus est meae puellae* keeps all eleven syllables — *-us* before *est* is just a short syllable.

Ørberg's rules (*Dē versibus*, paraphrased): a syllable ending in a short vowel is short; one ending in a long vowel, a diphthong or a consonant is long. The clusters *br, gr, cr, tr* usually begin a syllable (*li-brī*), so the vowel before them may stay short, but poets sometimes divide them (*nig-rōs*). A final consonant joins a following vowel (*a-nu-s‿est*). A final *-ō* is sometimes short (*volŏ, nēmŏ*). Two shorts equal one long in time, which is why a spondee can stand in for a dactyl.

Method for any line: copy it out, cross out elisions, write – over long vowels and diphthongs and over every vowel followed by two consonants, ⏑ over the rest, then divide from the end — the last two feet of a hexameter are almost always – ⏑ ⏑ | – x, the second half of a pentameter always – ⏑ ⏑ | – ⏑ ⏑ | –. The learner's notes have no page on prosody; Ørberg's Pēnsum A for chapter 34 sets two Martial couplets to scan.
'Long' means it takes longer to say, not that it is louder.
*x* counts as two consonants by itself, *h* as none. One softening: *br, cr, gr, tr* usually start the next syllable, so the vowel before them may stay short (*li-brī*).
One licence to know: a final *-ō* is sometimes counted short (*volŏ*, *nēmŏ*).

sources: Ørberg cap. XXXIV Grammatica Latina (Dē versibus)
